hints: Break the formula $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{COOH}$ into three sections, the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ end, the $\text{NH}_2$ branch, and the $\text{COOH}$ end.
Recall the Cambridge names for $\text{-COOH}$, $\text{-NH}_2$ attached to carbon, and $\text{C}=\text{C}$, remembering that $\text{COOH}$ is not just carbonyl or hydroxyl alone.
walkthrough:
Split the molecule into its reactive parts**
Look at $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{COOH}$ with me. On the left you have $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH-}$, in the middle a carbon carrying $\text{NH}_2$, and on the right $\text{COOH}$. Each of those is a different functional group, so treat them one at a time.

Name each group correctly**
The $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond makes it an alkene. The $\text{-NH}_2$ group attached to carbon is an amine, here a primary amine. The $\text{-COOH}$ group is a carboxylic acid, do not split it into separate carbonyl plus alcohol, Cambridge expects the whole group name.
Final answer: carboxylic acid, amine (primary amine) and alkene.

hints: Check the carbon in $\text{CH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{COOH}$, count how many different groups are attached to it to decide if H is chiral.
Recall how to show a pair of non-superimposable mirror images using solid wedge for out of the plane and dashed wedge for into the plane, plus the name for this type of stereoisomerism.
walkthrough:
Spot why H must be chiral**
Focus on the carbon in $\text{CH}(\text{NH}_2)$. It is bonded to four different things: $\text{H}$, $\text{NH}_2$, $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$. A carbon with four different groups is a chiral centre, so the molecule exists as two enantiomers.

Draw the mirror image pair in 3D**
Draw the central C with, say, $\text{COOH}$ at the top and $\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$ on the left. Then put $\text{NH}_2$ on a solid wedge (coming out) and $\text{H}$ on a dashed wedge (going back) for one isomer. For the second isomer, simply swap the wedge and dash positions of $\text{NH}_2$ and H to give the mirror image. This type is optical isomerism.

Final answer: Optical isomerism. Two 3D structures showing the chiral carbon bonded to $\text{COOH}$, $\text{NH}_2$, $\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$ and H, with wedge and dash bonds interchanged to give non-superimposable mirror images (enantiomers).

hints: Look at J in Fig. 6.1, it contains an amide link ($\text{-CO-NH-}$) and an ester link ($\text{-CO-O-}$) in the same six-membered ring, both are broken by hot aqueous acid.
walkthrough:
See J opening into two pieces**
Think of J as two acids joined head to tail. The ring has $\text{-CO-O-}$ (ester part) and $\text{-CO-NH-}$ (amide part). Hot aqueous acid adds water across both links, opening the ring completely. One fragment becomes H, $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{COOH}$, and the other becomes $\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH}$ (2-hydroxyethanoic acid). That is why $2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is needed on the left.

hints: Recall the name given when water splits ester or amide bonds under acidic or alkaline conditions.
walkthrough:
Link water splitting to the name**
Whenever water breaks a bond, with $\text{H}$ adding to one side and $\text{OH}$ to the other, and here it breaks both amide and ester links in J, chemists call it hydrolysis. Because hot aqueous acid is used, you can say acid hydrolysis.

hints: For addition polymer K, decide which functional group reacts (the $\text{C}=\text{C}$) and which groups ($\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{COOH}$) remain unchanged as side chains.
walkthrough:
Polymerise only the double bond**
For addition polymerisation, forget the $\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{COOH}$ for a moment, they just watch. The $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH-}$ double bond opens to a single bond and links to neighbours. So the backbone becomes $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH-} $ repeated, with the rest of the molecule, $\text{-CH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{COOH}$, hanging off as a side chain. Show continuation bonds at each end of the backbone.

Final answer: One repeat unit: $\text{-[CH}_2\text{-CH}(\text{CH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{COOH})\text{-}$ with continuation bonds through the backbone carbons, i.e. backbone $\text{CH}_2\text{-CH}$ carrying side chain $\text{CH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{COOH}$.

hints: For condensation polymer L, identify the two groups that react together ($\text{NH}_2$ of one H with $\text{COOH}$ of the next) and the small molecule lost.
Recall how to display the new amide link $\text{-CO-NH-}$ fully and how to join two monomer units head to tail to show two repeats.
walkthrough:
Form the amide link between monomers**
Now the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ just watches. The $\text{NH}_2$ end of one H attacks the $\text{COOH}$ end of the next H, losing $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to give $\text{-CO-NH-}$. That is the new functional group you must display in full, not just as CONH in shorthand without atoms clear.

Extend to two repeats**
Join them head to tail: $\text{-NH-CH}(\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2\text{)-C}(=\text{O}\text{)-}$ then repeat again $\text{-NH-CH}(\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2\text{)-C}(=\text{O}\text{)-}$. Keep the vinyl side chain $\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$ intact on each alpha carbon and put continuation bonds at both ends to show the chain continues.

Final answer: Two repeat units showing amide links displayed: $\text{-NH-CH}(\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2\text{)-CO-NH-CH}(\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2\text{)-CO-}$ with continuation bonds, amide $\text{-CO-NH-}$ shown in full.

hints: Compare the linkages in the backbone, polar amide ($\text{-CO-NH-}$) in L that can react with water versus non-polar $\text{C-C}$ in K.
walkthrough:
Connect linkage to breakdown**
Picture the backbones. L is held together by polar amide $\text{C-N}$ and $\text{C}=\text{O}$ bonds that water or enzymes can attack and split, reversing condensation. K is just a long chain of strong, non-polar $\text{C-C}$ bonds that water cannot break, so microbes cannot easily chop it into small pieces. That is why condensation polymers normally biodegrade more readily.

Final answer: Condensation polymers contain amide linkages that can be hydrolysed (by water, acids or enzymes), so the chain can be broken down, whereas addition polymers have an inert hydrocarbon C-C backbone.
